title: What a p-value does and does not mean
learning_objectives: Interpret a p-value as a probability conditional on a statistical model and observed-or-more-extreme data.
Reject the claim that a p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Separate statistical evidence from effect size and practical importance.

sources.title: The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose

misconceptions.description: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A smaller p-value necessarily means a larger or more important effect.

critical_errors.description: Defines the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Claims that statistical significance alone establishes practical importance or causality.

teaching_brief.goal: Help the learner interpret p-values without reversing the conditional probability.
teaching_brief.learner_profile: An undergraduate who has seen hypothesis tests but confuses P(data | null) with P(null | data).
instructions: Diagnose the learner's current interpretation before explaining.
Use one concrete example and explicitly name what is held conditional.
Ask the learner to restate the meaning in their own words.
Contrast evidence, effect size, and practical importance.
prohibited_disclosures: Do not show or infer any held-out assessment item.
Do not state that a p-value is a posterior probability for a hypothesis.

pretest.prompt: A study reports p = 0.04 under a null hypothesis. Which interpretation is closest?

choices.text: The null hypothesis has a 4% probability of being true.
If the null model were true, data at least this incompatible would occur with probability 4%.
There is a 96% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
The observed effect has a 4% probability of being caused by chance.

pretest.prompt: Two large studies report p = 0.001 for effects of very different sizes. What follows from the p-values alone?

choices.text: Both effects are equally large.
Both effects are practically important.
Neither effect size nor practical importance is determined by the p-values alone.
Both studies prove a causal effect.

posttest.prompt: A test gives p = 0.02. Which probability is directly described?

choices.text: P(null hypothesis is true | observed data)
P(observed-or-more-extreme data | null model)
P(researcher made an error | observed data)
P(result will replicate | observed data)

posttest.prompt: A tiny treatment effect has p < 0.001 in a sample of one million. What is still needed to judge importance?

choices.text: Only a smaller significance threshold
Effect size, uncertainty, and domain consequences
A second p-value below 0.001
Nothing; the p-value establishes importance

transfer.prompt: A diagnostic algorithm differs from a baseline with p = 0.049 but improves accuracy by 0.01 percentage points. Which conclusion is defensible?

choices.text: The algorithm is certainly useful because p < 0.05.
The null hypothesis is false with probability 95.1%.
The data meet the chosen significance rule, but usefulness requires effect-size and cost analysis.
The improvement cannot be sampling variation.

transfer.prompt: What additional framework would be needed to assign a probability to a hypothesis after observing data?

choices.text: A Bayesian model with prior assumptions and a likelihood
A larger font for the p-value
A rule that p must be below 0.05
A random-number generator

retention.prompt: Complete the statement: a p-value is computed assuming...

choices.text: the tested statistical model, including the null, is true
the alternative hypothesis is certainly true
the observed effect is practically important
the experiment has no bias

retention.prompt: Which pair must not be treated as the same quantity?

choices.text: Sample size and number of observations
P(data | hypothesis) and P(hypothesis | data)
Mean and average in ordinary arithmetic
0.05 and five percent
